summary: Four problems from the interview-lab days that belong to no single Section 4 topic. They are here so the Heaps and Graphs chapters stay clean, not because they share a technique. Each one is a different reflex: a hash map remembering the last position of a value, a sliding window with character counts, a greedy that sums every upward move, and a construction that reads a binary counter as a palindrome. Recognising which reflex applies from the problem statement is the whole exercise.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. 'Closest / nearest equal pair' -> hash map of last seen index.
thoughtProcess.body: One pass, and for each value keep the most recent index you saw it at. The closest pair ending at i always uses the LAST occurrence before i, never an older one, so a single map entry per value is enough. O(N) time, O(N) space.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. 'Smallest window containing all of X' -> two pointers with counts.
thoughtProcess.body: Expand the right edge until the window is valid, then shrink the left edge while it stays valid, recording the best. A single 'how many required characters are still missing' counter is cheaper and less bug-prone than comparing two maps every step.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Unlimited buy/sell -> add up every upward move.
thoughtProcess.body: With no limit on transactions, the maximum profit is the sum of all positive consecutive differences. You never need to find peaks and valleys explicitly -- every rise is capturable and every fall is skippable.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. 'A-th thing in a generated sequence' -> look for a bijection, not a search.
thoughtProcess.body: When the A-th object has structure (a palindrome built from a binary counter), construct it directly from A instead of enumerating and filtering. Enumeration is exponential; the construction is O(log A).

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Read what the counts are actually keyed on.
thoughtProcess.body: These problems all hinge on one bookkeeping decision: last index vs first index, characters remaining vs characters seen, difference vs absolute value. Getting that wrong produces code that passes the samples and fails the edges.

keyPatterns.name: Last-seen index map (closest equal pair)
keyPatterns.when: Minimum distance between two equal values, or 'has a duplicate within K'.

keyPatterns.name: Sliding window with a 'missing' counter
keyPatterns.when: Smallest / longest window satisfying a multiset condition.

keyPatterns.name: Sum of positive differences (unlimited transactions)
keyPatterns.when: Buy/sell any number of times, maximise profit.
examples: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stocks II

keyPatterns.name: Construct the A-th object from its index
keyPatterns.when: The sequence has structure; enumerating it would be exponential.

commonMistakes.title: Keeping the FIRST index instead of the last
commonMistakes.why: For a minimum distance you want the nearest previous occurrence. Holding the first index makes every later comparison measure to the wrong end and reports a distance that is too large.

commonMistakes.title: Decrementing the window deficit for characters you do not need
commonMistakes.why: Characters outside the target, or extra copies beyond what is required, must not reduce the deficit. If they do, the window reports itself valid early and you return a window that is too short.

commonMistakes.title: Hunting for explicit peaks and valleys in the stock problem
commonMistakes.wrong: find each local min, find the next local max, add the difference
commonMistakes.right: for (i = 1..n-1) if (A[i] > A[i-1]) profit += A[i] - A[i-1];
commonMistakes.why: The telescoping sum of consecutive rises equals the peak-minus-valley total, and the one-liner has no edge cases at the ends of the array or on plateaus.

commonMistakes.title: Comparing two frequency maps on every window step
commonMistakes.why: Map equality is O(alphabet) per step, turning an O(N) scan into O(N * 256). A scalar deficit counter keeps each step O(1).

edgeCases: No duplicate at all in Shaggy -- return -1 rather than Integer.MAX_VALUE.
Adjacent duplicates give distance 1, the smallest possible; do not skip i - 1.
Window source shorter than the target string -- return an empty string immediately.
Target containing repeated characters: the window needs that many copies, not one.
Strictly decreasing prices -- profit is 0, never negative.
Single-element price array -- the loop body never runs, return 0.
A = 1 for Perfect Numbers -- the smallest member of the family, check it by hand.
Very large A where the constructed string exceeds int range -- build a string, never a number.
Empty input array or string in any of the four -- guard before the first index access.
